title: Caring for our environment: why some litter traps animals, and what we can do

summary.text: A loop of wet newspaper tears at one gentle pull, but a loop cut from a milk packet only stretches and holds. That is why plastic litter can trap a bird, a cow or a turtle, and paper usually cannot. Your child soaks loops of paper, cloth and plastic in water and tries to pull each one apart. Then we find out how litter harms the animals who live around us, and the real ways families, villages and cities in India care for their environment.
summary.art: A child at a kitchen table pulling apart a wet paper loop that tears, while a plastic loop from a milk packet lies stretched but whole beside a steel bowl of water.

intro.hook: On the day after a kite festival, people in many Indian cities find birds caught in kite string on trees and balconies. Why can't the bird just break the string and fly away?
intro.text: A bird cannot break some kinds of string, however hard the bird pulls. Strong plastic litter can trap animals the same way. Our environment is everything around us: the air, the water, the land and every living being. In this unit we test which kinds of litter can trap an animal. Then we learn what people in India do to care for the places we share.
intro.art: A pigeon sitting on a balcony railing with a piece of kite string looped round one foot, and a girl looking at the bird from behind the glass door.

outcomes: By the end I can say what our environment is, and name living and non-living parts of it.
By the end I can say how litter harms animals: they can get trapped in it, or eat it.
By the end I can test which loops of litter break when wet and which stay strong, and say what I found.
By the end I can say why plastic litter is a bigger danger to animals than paper litter.
By the end I can name three ways to care for our environment at home, such as snipping loops and using a cloth bag.
By the end I can tell a true story of Indian people, many of them women, who cared for trees, birds or beaches.

terms.meaning: Our environment is everything around us: air, water, land, plants, animals and people.
terms.example: Your building, the road, the neem tree outside, the crows and the drain are all part of your environment.
terms.art: A city street with a building, a neem tree, crows, a dog, a drain, and the sky above, all labelled as one environment.

terms.meaning: Litter is rubbish left in the wrong place, outside a bin.
terms.example: A chips packet on the pavement and a plastic bag in a lake are litter.
terms.art: A chips packet and a plastic bag lying on a pavement beside a bin.

terms.meaning: An animal is trapped when they are caught in something and cannot get free.
terms.example: A pigeon with kite string wound round their foot is trapped.
terms.art: A pigeon on a branch with a string wound round one foot.

terms.meaning: Plastic is a material made by people, mostly from oil or gas. Most plastic is strong, light and does not soak up water.
terms.example: Milk packets, carry bags, straws and nylon string are made of plastic.
terms.art: A milk packet, a carry bag, a straw and a reel of nylon string on a table.

terms.meaning: A habitat is the place where a living being lives and finds what they need.
terms.example: A lake is a habitat for fish, frogs, ducks and lotus plants.
terms.art: A lake with lotus plants, ducks on the water and fish under the surface.

terms.meaning: To protect means to keep someone or something safe from harm.
terms.example: Women in Assam protect the nests of big storks in their village trees.
terms.art: Women standing under a tall tree with big stork nests at the top.

explanations.context: This card says what the word environment means.
explanations.definition: Our environment is everything around us. It has living parts and non-living parts.
explanations.description: The living parts are plants, animals, fungi and tiny microbes. People are animals too, so we are part of it. The non-living parts are air, water, soil, rock and sunlight. Every being needs the others to live.
examples: A crow needs trees for a nest and clean water to drink.
A neem tree needs soil, sunlight, rain and air.
You need clean air, clean water and food that grew in soil.
explanations.art: A circle showing a crow, a neem tree, a child, the Sun, a raincloud and soil, with arrows joining them.

explanations.context: This card says the two main ways litter hurts animals.
explanations.definition: Litter harms animals in two main ways. They get trapped in it, or they eat it.
explanations.description: Birds get caught in kite string and in loops of plastic. Cows on Indian streets eat plastic bags that have food scraps inside. Vets have taken heaps of plastic out of cows' stomachs. Turtles in the sea can swallow floating bags.
examples: A pigeon with kite string wound round a foot.
A cow eating a plastic bag with vegetable peels inside.
A dog cutting a paw on broken glass.
explanations.art: Three small pictures: a pigeon caught in string, a cow eating a plastic bag, and a turtle near a floating bag.

explanations.concept: Why plastic is the most dangerous litter
explanations.context: Remember the wet loop test, where you soaked loops of paper, cloth and plastic? This card says what it shows.
explanations.definition: Plastic stays strong in water and does not rot away quickly. So a plastic loop or string can trap an animal for a long time.
explanations.description: Water makes paper soft and weak, so a wet paper loop tears. Plastic does not soak up water, so it stays strong. Paper and cotton rot away in weeks or months. Most plastic lasts for many years, breaking only into smaller and smaller pieces.
examples: A wet paper bag tears, but a wet plastic bag does not.
Cotton kite string breaks more easily than nylon string, which is a plastic.
A plastic bag can float in a lake for years.
explanations.art: A torn wet paper loop next to a whole, stretched plastic loop, beside a bowl of water.

explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists are still working on: how long does plastic last?
explanations.description: Everyone agrees that most plastic lasts much longer than paper, cloth or peels. But nobody has watched a plastic bag for hundreds of years, because plastic bags are only about 60 years old. So the numbers are careful guesses.
examples: A plastic bag left in sunlight cracks into small bits, but the bits stay.
A plastic bottle in the sea can last a very long time.

perspectives.explanation: Plastic breaks into tiny pieces in sunlight and waves, and those pieces may last hundreds of years.
Some plastics may break down faster than we thought, for example in strong sunlight. The time depends on the kind of plastic and where it is.

explanations.art: A plastic bag shown at four times: whole, cracked, in pieces, and as tiny bits in sand.

explanations.concept: Ways we can care for our environment
explanations.context: This card says what a family can really do to care for the place we share.
explanations.definition: We care for our environment when we keep litter out of it, use less plastic, and protect the beings who live in it.
explanations.description: Put litter in a bin, and sort it into wet and dry waste. Snip every loop before you throw it away, so the loop cannot trap an animal. Carry a cloth bag. Keep a bowl of water for birds in summer. Plant trees and look after them.
examples: Snip a rubber band before it goes in the bin.
Fly kites with cotton string, not nylon string.
Pick up kite string left on the terrace after the festival.
explanations.art: A family at home: one child snipping a rubber band with scissors, a parent holding a cloth bag, and a water bowl on the balcony with a sparrow drinking.

explanations.concept: People in India who cared for the places they live
explanations.context: This card tells three true stories of people in India who protected trees and birds.
explanations.definition: People in India have protected trees and birds by working together, and many of them were women.
explanations.description: In 1974, Gaura Devi and the women of Reni village hugged the trees so that loggers could not cut them down. This was part of the Chipko movement. Chipko means to hug or to stick to. In Assam, Purnima Devi Barman, a scientist who studies birds, started the Hargila Army. Thousands of village women now protect the nests of the greater adjutant stork, called hargila in Assamese. In Karnataka, Saalumarada Thimmakka planted banyan trees along about 4 kilometres of road and looked after them.
examples: The women of Reni village held on to the trees, and the loggers went away.
The Hargila Army guards the nesting trees of a rare stork.
Thimmakka's banyan trees are now giant trees beside a road.
explanations.art: Women with their arms round a tall tree in a hill village, a stork on a nest in a village tree, and a long road lined with big banyan trees.

agreed.text: Litter harms many animals, by trapping them or when they eat it.
agreed.evidence: Vets and bird rescuers in India treat birds cut by kite string and cows sick from eating plastic bags. Scientists find plastic in the stomachs of many sea birds and turtles.

agreed.text: Plastic lasts far longer in water and soil than paper, cloth or peels.
agreed.evidence: In your wet loop test, the paper tore and the plastic held. Tests that bury things in soil find peels and paper rotting in weeks, while plastic looks the same.

agreed.text: Nylon kite string is dangerous to birds and people.
agreed.evidence: In 2017 India's National Green Tribunal, a court for the environment, banned nylon and other plastic kite string across the country, because it was hurting birds, other animals and people.

challenging.claim: A little bit of litter does no harm.
challenging.for: One wrapper looks small, and a sweeper may pick it up.
challenging.against: One loop of string can trap one bird. Many people each dropping a little make a lot of litter, and rain carries it into drains and lakes.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that one small piece of litter does not matter.

challenging.claim: Paper bags are always better for the environment than plastic bags.
challenging.for: Paper rots away in weeks and does not trap animals for years.
challenging.against: Making a paper bag uses trees, water and energy, often more than a thin plastic bag. A cloth bag used many, many times is better than both. Scientists still argue about which bag is best overall.
challenging.context: This card is about paper bags and plastic bags: which is better?

challenging.claim: Caring for the environment is only the government's job.
challenging.for: Cities have sweepers, laws and big trucks for waste. A family is small.
challenging.against: Laws help a lot, but ordinary people have also saved forests, birds and beaches. The women of Reni village saved their forest, and the women of the Hargila Army saved a rare stork.
challenging.context: This card is about who should care for our environment.

big_questions.q: Why did the wet paper tear, but the wet plastic did not?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the water did to each one. Did the water go into the plastic?

big_questions.q: Why does a cow eat a plastic bag?
big_questions.hint: What was inside the bag? What does it smell of?

big_questions.q: Who does the lake belong to: the people who live near it, or the fish, frogs and birds in the lake too?
big_questions.hint: Who needs the lake every day, and for what?

big_questions.q: If nobody sees you drop a wrapper, does it still matter?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the wrapper goes next, and who might meet it there.

story.title: The String on the Balcony
story.note: Meenakshi, Arun, Amma and Dr. Rehana are made up. Kite flying at Sankranti is a big festival in Hyderabad and in many parts of India. Nylon kite string was banned in India in 2017 because it hurts birds and people. If you find a trapped bird, call an animal rescue group or a vet, and do not try to pull the string yourself.
text: Meenakshi lived on the sixth floor of a building in Hyderabad. She was seven. Her little brother Arun was five.
It was Sankranti, the kite festival. All day, the sky was full of kites. Red kites, green kites and kites with long paper tails flew over every roof.
Arun loved the kites. "I want to fly one too!" he said.
The next morning, Meenakshi heard a strange flapping sound on the balcony. She looked out through the glass door.

A grey pigeon was sitting on the railing. A long piece of kite string was wound round one of the pigeon's feet. The other end was caught on a nail in the wall. The pigeon flapped and pulled, flapped and pulled. But the string did not break.
"Amma!" Meenakshi called. "A pigeon is caught!"
Amma came quickly. She looked at the string. "We must not pull it," she said. "Pulling can cut the pigeon's foot. Let us call Dr. Rehana."
Dr. Rehana was a vet who lived in the next building. She looked after hurt birds and other animals. She came up in ten minutes, with a towel and a small pair of scissors.
She put the towel gently over the pigeon. The pigeon went still under the soft dark cloth. Then she snipped the string, bit by bit, until the foot was free.
"This foot is only a little red," said Dr. Rehana. "She was lucky. You called me fast."
Arun looked at the string in her hand. "Why didn't the pigeon just break the string?" he asked. "She pulled so hard."
"Feel it," said Dr. Rehana. Arun pulled the string. It did not break. It cut into his fingers a little, so he stopped.
"This string is made of nylon," said Dr. Rehana. "Nylon is a kind of plastic. It is very strong, even when it is wet. A bird cannot break nylon string."
She took the towel off. The pigeon stood up, shook her feathers, and flew to the next roof.
That evening, Meenakshi had an idea. She cut a strip from an old newspaper and a strip from an empty milk packet. She tied each one into a loop and put both loops in a bowl of water.
After ten minutes she took out the paper loop and pulled it gently. It tore at once. Then she pulled the plastic loop. It stretched and went thin, but it did not tear.
"Look, Arun," said Meenakshi. "A wet paper loop could never trap a bird. But a plastic loop could."
Arun pulled the plastic loop too. "It is like the kite string," he said.
The next day, Meenakshi went up to the terrace with Amma. Bits of kite string hung from the water tank and the TV dish. They lay in tangles on the floor.
Meenakshi showed Arun how to pick them up and wind them round a stick. "Every bit we pick up is one less trap," she said.
They filled a whole bag. Arun counted the sticks of wound string. There were eleven.
"Next Sankranti," said Arun, "can I fly a kite with cotton string?"
"Yes," said Amma. "And we will fly it in the middle of the day, when fewer birds are flying. And we will pick up every bit of string when we finish."
On the railing, the grey pigeon was back, pecking at a few grains of rice. Both her feet were free.
story.epiphany: A loop that a bird cannot break is a trap. Plastic stays strong even when wet, so plastic string and loops can trap animals. Picking them up keeps the birds safe.
ask: Why did Dr. Rehana snip the string instead of pulling it?
Why did the paper loop tear but the plastic loop did not?
What could Meenakshi's family do at the next Sankranti to keep birds safe?
art: A city sky full of colourful kites over the roofs of Hyderabad on Sankranti.
A grey pigeon on a balcony railing with kite string wound round one foot and caught on a nail.
A woman vet with a towel over the pigeon, gently snipping the string with small scissors.
A girl pulling a wet paper loop that tears, and a plastic loop that only stretches.
A girl and her small brother on a terrace winding found kite string round sticks.

experiments.title: The Wet Loop Test: which litter could a bird pull free from?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make loops from paper, cloth and plastic. You soak them in water, like litter in a lake or a puddle. Then you try to pull each loop apart, the way a trapped bird would.
experiments.question: After a soak in water, which loops tear when you pull them gently: paper, cloth or plastic? Which loops stay whole?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which wet loop will tear: paper, cloth or plastic? Which will stay whole? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every strip is the same size: two fingers wide and as long as a school ruler. Every wet loop soaks for the same 10 minutes. You pull every loop the same gentle way, up to 5 pulls. We also keep one dry paper loop, so we can see what the water did to the paper.
results_table: My guess: tear or stay whole?
Number of pulls before it tore (stop at 5)
What it looked like at the end

materials.item: strips of old newspaper, two fingers wide and as long as a school ruler
a strip of old cotton cloth, such as an old vest or a torn dupatta, the same size
an empty milk packet, washed, cut into a strip the same size
a steel bowl of water
scissors (a grown-up cuts)
a pencil and paper for the table

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the strips. Pull gently with your fingers. Stop if a loop pinches or cuts into your fingers.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the four loops after the test, showing which ones tore.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from one family in Visakhapatnam

setup.art: A grown-up's hands cutting a strip from a washed milk packet, with a newspaper strip and a cloth strip of the same size on the table.
setup.caption: 1. Cut four strips of the same size: two paper, one cloth, one plastic.

setup.art: A child tying each strip into a loop with one knot, with four loops in a row.
setup.caption: 2. Tie each strip into a loop with one knot.

setup.art: Three loops sinking in a steel bowl of water, and one dry paper loop beside the bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Put three loops in water for 10 minutes. Keep one paper loop dry.

setup.art: A child with a wet loop hooked over two fingers of each hand, gently pulling the hands apart.
setup.caption: 4. Hook a loop over your fingers and pull gently. Count the pulls.

flow.do: 1. Cut two newspaper strips, one cloth strip and one milk-packet strip, all the same size. 2. Help your child tie each strip into a loop with one knot.
flow.say: These loops are like litter. A bird or a cow could get a foot or a neck caught in a loop. Let's find out which loops they could break.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts four strips. Tie each one into a loop.
flow.parent: Make the strips two fingers wide and about 30 centimetres long. Tie the paper loop loosely, so it does not tear while you knot it. Cut the milk packet smoothly, with no nicks in the edge, because a nick can make the plastic tear. Lift the wet paper loop out gently, so it does not tear before the test.

flow.do: Hold up each loop. Ask for a guess and a reason for each. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: We will soak three loops in water, like litter in a lake. Which wet loop will tear when you pull it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which wet loop will tear? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which wet loop will tear? Why?
good: The paper, because water makes paper soft.
None of them, because they are all strong.
The cloth, because it soaks up water.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Write it down with the reason. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Put the paper, cloth and plastic loops in the bowl. 2. Push them under the water. 3. Keep the second paper loop dry on the table. 4. Wait 10 minutes.
flow.say: While we wait, let's look. Which loop is soaking up water? Which one is floating? Draw the bowl.
flow.kid: Put three loops in the water. Wait 10 minutes. Keep one paper loop dry.
flow.parent: Use the 10 minutes to draw the bowl, or to read the story. The plastic strip may float, so push it under now and then.

flow.do: 1. Start with the dry paper loop. 2. Your child hooks the loop over two fingers of each hand. 3. They pull their hands apart gently, up to 5 times. 4. Do the same with each wet loop. 5. Write the number of pulls.
flow.say: Pull gently, like a bird trying to get free. Count each pull. Stop at 5, or when the loop tears.
flow.kid: Hook a loop over your fingers. Pull gently. Count each pull.
flow.parent: The wet paper usually tears at the first or second pull. The dry paper, the cloth and the plastic usually hold for all 5 pulls. The plastic stretches and goes thin, but stays whole. If the plastic pinches, stop.

flow.do: Fill in the table together. Ask your child three things: what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which loop tore? Which loops stayed whole? Look at the two paper loops. What did the water do to the paper?
flow.kid: Look at your table. What did you find? Why?
flow.think: A pigeon gets a foot caught in a wet plastic loop in a puddle. Can she pull free?

check.q: Which wet loop tore when you pulled it?
check.why: Water soaks into paper and makes it soft, so the wet paper tore. The dry paper held, so the water made the difference. Plastic does not soak up water, so it stayed strong. A bird could pull free from wet paper, but not from plastic.

experiments.title: Bag in the Bucket: does a floating plastic bag look like a living animal?
experiments.context: Some sea turtles eat jellyfish. Jellyfish are soft, see-through animals who float and drift in the sea. In this experiment you put a thin plastic bag in a bucket of water and watch how it moves. You compare it with paper and cloth.
experiments.question: In water, does a thin plastic bag look and move like a floating jellyfish? Do paper and cloth look like that too?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which one will look most like a floating jellyfish: the plastic bag, the paper or the cloth? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each thing goes into the same bucket of water. You stir the water the same way, three slow turns with a spoon. You watch each one from the side for the same time, one minute.
results_table: My guess: looks like a jellyfish?
Does it float, sink or drift?
Does it look like a jellyfish? Draw it.

materials.item: a bucket of water, or a big steel vessel
a thin, clear or white plastic carry bag
a sheet of newspaper
a white cotton handkerchief
a long spoon
a picture of a jellyfish from a book or a phone, or draw one: a round soft dome with long thin arms hanging down

experiments.record: Draw each thing in the water, and the jellyfish picture next to them.

setup.art: A bucket of water on a bathroom floor, with a thin white plastic bag, a newspaper sheet and a handkerchief beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Fill a bucket with water.

setup.art: A thin plastic bag drifting under the water in the bucket, puffed open like a jellyfish, seen from the side.
setup.caption: 2. Put in one thing at a time. Stir slowly and watch from the side.

setup.art: A child comparing a drawing of the floating bag with a picture of a jellyfish.
setup.caption: 3. Compare each one with a jellyfish picture.

flow.do: Show a picture of a jellyfish, or draw one: a round soft dome with long thin arms hanging down. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Some sea turtles eat jellyfish. Which of these three will look most like a jellyfish in water? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the jellyfish picture. Guess which thing will look like a jellyfish. Why?

ask.q: Which one will look like a jellyfish? Why?
good: The plastic bag, because it is thin and see-through.
The cloth, because it is white and soft.

flow.do: 1. Put the plastic bag in the water. Push it under once. 2. Stir three slow turns. 3. Watch from the side for one minute. 4. Take it out. Do the same with the paper, then the cloth.
flow.say: Watch the bag from the side, like a turtle under the water. Does it float, sink or drift? Does it look alive?
flow.kid: Put in one thing at a time. Stir slowly. Watch from the side.
flow.parent: A thin bag usually puffs open and drifts slowly in the middle of the water, much like a jellyfish. It may not do this every time. If the bag only lies flat on top, push it under with the spoon and let go. The newspaper goes soggy and sinks or tears. The handkerchief sinks or lies flat.

flow.do: Compare your child's drawings with the jellyfish picture.
flow.say: Which one looked most like a jellyfish? What might a hungry turtle do if she saw the bag?
flow.kid: Which one looked most like a jellyfish? Why might a turtle eat the bag?

check.q: Which one drifted and looked most like a jellyfish?
check.why: The thin bag puffed open and drifted, like a jellyfish. Scientists have found plastic bags in the stomachs of sea turtles. Many think the turtles mistake the bags for jellyfish, though they are still studying how often this happens.

experiments.safety: Stay with your child at the bucket. Keep the plastic bag away from faces, and away from babies and pets. Empty the bucket when you finish.

activities.title: Loop Hunt: find the traps in our dry waste
activities.context: In this activity you look through one day's dry waste for loops and strings that could trap an animal. Then you snip each loop open.

materials.item: one day's clean dry waste from your home
child-safe scissors
an old newspaper to spread out

activities.safety: Use only clean, dry waste. Leave out anything sharp, such as broken glass or tins. Wash hands with soap after. A grown-up snips any used mask.
activities.record: Make a tally mark for each loop you find and snip.

setup.art: A child and a parent spreading dry waste on a newspaper on the floor: packets, a rubber band, a mask, a string.
setup.caption: 1. Spread the dry waste on a newspaper.

setup.art: A child snipping a rubber band open with child-safe scissors, with tally marks on a paper beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Snip every loop open. Make a tally mark.

flow.do: Spread one day's clean dry waste on a newspaper. Your child looks for anything shaped like a loop or a long string.
flow.say: Look for loops and strings. A bird's foot or a dog's nose could get stuck in them.
flow.kid: Spread the dry waste out. Look for loops and strings.
flow.parent: Common loops are rubber bands, mask ear loops, the rings on packets, plastic strapping from parcels and pieces of string. Hard plastic strapping is tough, so a grown-up snips it.

flow.do: Your child snips each loop open, so it becomes a straight strip. Make a tally mark for each one.
flow.say: Snip it open. Now it is a strip, not a loop. Can a bird's foot get stuck in the strip now?
flow.kid: Snip each loop open. Make a tally mark for each one.

good: A strip cannot close round a foot.
An animal can pull free from a strip.

flow.do: Count the tally marks together. Put the waste back in the dry waste bin.
flow.say: How many traps did we find in one day? How many might we find in a week?
flow.kid: Count your marks. Put the waste back in the dry bin.

activities.title: Spot the Care: three places near home
activities.context: In this activity you look at three places near your home, from a window or on a short walk with a grown-up. For each place, you say whether people have cared for it, and how it could be better.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Look at litter, but do not touch it. Stay with a grown-up outside.
activities.record: Draw a table with three rows: the place, a smiling or sad face, and one way to make it better.

setup.art: A girl at a window with a notebook, looking down at a parking area, a street and a small garden.
setup.caption: 1. Choose three places you can see or visit.

setup.art: A notebook page with three rows: a parking area with a sad face, a street with a sad face, a garden with a smiling face, and ideas written beside each.
setup.caption: 2. Give each place a face and one idea.

flow.do: Choose three places, such as the parking area, the street and a garden or the building's entrance.
flow.say: Before we look, guess. Which place will be the cleanest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Choose three places. Guess which one is cared for best.

flow.do: Look at each place for 2 or 3 minutes. Your child looks for litter, plants and animals, and draws a face.
flow.say: Is there litter here? Is there anything that could trap an animal? Do any plants or animals live here?
flow.kid: Look at each place. Is there litter? Are there plants and animals?

flow.do: For each place, your child says one way to make it better, and who could help.
flow.say: How could we make this place better? Who could help us?
flow.kid: Say one way to make each place better.

good: The building's watchman or the society.
The city's sweepers and waste workers.

activities.title: Terrace String Sweep (after a kite festival, if you have a terrace)
activities.context: After Sankranti, Uttarayan or any kite day, kite string is left on roofs, tanks and trees. In this activity you wind up the string you find, so birds cannot get caught in it.

materials.item: a few sticks or empty cardboard tubes
a bag

activities.safety: Go to the terrace only with a grown-up, and keep away from the edge. Do not climb to reach string. A grown-up handles any glass-coated or nylon string, which can cut.
activities.record: Count the sticks of wound string.

setup.art: A parent and child on a terrace finding tangled kite string near a water tank.
setup.caption: 1. Look for string on the floor, tanks and railings.

setup.art: A child winding string round a stick while a parent cuts a tangled bit free.
setup.caption: 2. Wind it round a stick. Count the sticks.

flow.do: Look on the floor, on tanks and on railings. Wind each piece round a stick.
flow.say: Every bit of string we pick up is one less trap for a bird.
flow.kid: Find kite string. Wind it round a stick.
flow.parent: Do not reach over the edge or into trees. If you see a trapped bird, call a vet or an animal rescue group.

flow.do: Count the sticks together. Put the string in a bag in the dry waste.
flow.say: How many sticks did we fill? Where could this string have ended up?
flow.kid: Count your sticks. Put the string in the dry waste.

games.title: Trap, Swallow or Safe? A card sorting game
games.context: This is a card game about litter. Each card names a piece of litter. You say whether that litter could trap an animal, be swallowed, cut an animal, or is safer. Then you turn the card over to check.

items.b: Trap card. Birds get caught. Snip it and wind it up.
Trap card. A small loop can close round a bird's foot. Snip it.
Trap card. Snip the loops before you throw it away.

items.f: A plastic bag with peels inside
items.b: Swallow card. Cows eat it for the food smell. Empty peels into wet waste.
Swallow card. A turtle may think the bag is a jellyfish.
Swallow card. Sea birds may swallow small bright plastic bits.
Cut card. A dog or a cow can cut a paw or a foot.
Safer card. Wet paper tears and rots away soon. Still, put it in the bin.
Safer card. Peels rot into soil. They belong in the wet waste or compost.
Trap card. Turtles and fish get caught in lost nets.
Swallow card. Animals lick it for the salt and oil, and may swallow it.
Safer card. Cotton breaks more easily and rots away. Still, pick it up.

rules: Put the 4 sorting cards in a row on the floor.
Mix the litter cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over the top litter card and read the front aloud.
Put the card under the sorting card you think is right, and say why.
Turn the card over and read the back. If you were right, keep the card. If not, put the card in the middle, and nobody keeps it.
When the pile is gone, the player with the most cards wins. If players tie, they share the win. Then everyone says one way to stop each kind of harm.

options: The band could close round the bird's foot and trap the bird
The band could make the bird too heavy to fly
The band could make the bird's feathers wet
check.why: A rubber band is a strong loop. It can close round a bird's foot or beak. Snipping it open makes it a strip, which cannot close round anything.

rules: Put one litter token on each of the 10 spots. Put the raincloud token on rain step 1.
Mix the action cards and put them face down in a pile.

projects.title: Our Loop-Free Week
projects.context: In this project your family snips every loop and string before it goes in the bin, for one week. You count them each day, to see how many traps one home makes.

materials.item: child-safe scissors kept by the dry waste bin
a tally sheet on the fridge or wall

projects.record: A tally sheet with one row for each day of the week, and a total at the end.

schedule.what: Put scissors and a tally sheet by the dry bin. Tell everyone at home the plan.
Add up the week. Draw a poster for neighbours.

flow.do: Hang child-safe scissors and a tally sheet by the dry waste bin. Your child tells each person at home the plan.

check.q: Why do we snip loops before they go in the bin?
options: So an animal at the dump cannot get trapped in them
check.why: Waste from bins often ends up at open dumps, where cows, dogs and birds search for food. A snipped loop is a strip that cannot close round a foot or a neck.

challenges.title: A Kite Day That Is Safe for Birds
challenges.context: In this challenge you plan a kite festival day for your family that is fun for people and safe for birds.
challenges.problem: Your family wants to fly kites at Sankranti, or on any kite day. Plan the day so that no bird gets hurt.
constraints: Your plan must say what string to use, when to fly, and what to do after.
It must still be fun to fly kites.
Draw your plan on one sheet of paper.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and colours

setup.caption: 1. Draw your kite-day plan.

setup.caption: 2. Check that the plan keeps birds safe.

general: Use cotton string, not nylon or glass-coated string.
Pick up and wind up every bit of string after flying.
Do not fly kites near trees, where string gets caught.
creative: Fly kites in the middle of the day. Bird groups ask people to avoid early morning and evening, when many birds fly to and from their roosts.
Make a string collection box for the whole building.
Make a poster with the phone number of a nearby bird rescue group.
challenges.your_turn: What else could make your kite day safe for birds? Add one idea of your own.

flow.kid: Read the problem. What hurts birds on a kite day?

ask.q: What hurts birds on a kite day?
good: String left in trees and on roofs.
Flying kites when birds are flying.

check.q: Which kite string is safest for birds?
check.why: Plain cotton string breaks more easily and rots away. Nylon string is plastic, so it is very strong and lasts a long time. Glass-coated string cuts. India banned nylon kite string in 2017.

items.p: Draw the four loops after the wet loop test. Show which ones tore and which stayed whole.
items.a: A drawing with the wet paper loop torn, and the dry paper, cloth and plastic loops whole. The plastic loop may look stretched.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the torn wet paper and the stretched but whole plastic.

items.p: Draw a line from each piece of litter to the harm it can do.
items.why: String and loops trap. Bags with food smells get eaten. Glass cuts. Turtles may think a floating bag is a jellyfish.
items.art: Four kinds of litter on the left and four animals on the right, with dots to join.

items.p: Our environment is only the trees and the animals. People are not part of it.
items.why: False. Our environment is everything around us, living and non-living. People are animals, so we are part of it too.

items.p: A banana peel can close round a bird's foot and trap the bird, like a rubber band can.
items.why: False. A peel is soft and rots away into soil. A rubber band is a strong loop that can close round a foot.

items.p: Sort these into living and non-living parts of the environment.
items.why: Trees, crows and people grow, feed and have young. Water, soil and sunlight are not alive, but every living being needs them.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: why is a plastic loop more dangerous to a bird than a paper loop?
items.a: Plastic stays strong when wet, so a bird cannot break free. Paper tears when wet, so a bird could break free.
items.why: A strong answer uses the wet loop test as evidence.

items.p: Priya, a girl in Class 2, found these in her family's dry waste: 3 rubber bands, 2 masks with 2 loops each, and 1 packet with no loops. How many loops did she need to snip?
items.why: 3 rubber bands make 3 loops. 2 masks with 2 loops each make 4 loops. 3 + 4 = 7. The packet has no loops.

items.p: To keep birds safe, we ___ every loop open before it goes in the bin.
items.why: A snipped loop becomes a strip, which cannot close round a foot or a neck.

items.p: Two friends in Chennai are going shopping for vegetables.

views.says: Let's take a paper bag. Paper rots away and does not trap animals.
Let's take our cloth bag. We can use it again and again, so we make no litter at all.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: Either side, with a reason. Divya is right that paper rots away and tears when wet, so an animal is less likely to get trapped. Ammu is right that a bag used many times makes the least waste.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason from the unit for one side, and fairly says what the other side has right.

items.p: Look at the picture of a balcony. Label two things that could harm a bird, and one thing that helps a bird.
items.a: Harm: kite string on the railing, a rubber band on the floor. Help: a bowl of clean water.
items.why: A strong answer finds the loops or strings as traps and the water bowl as care.
items.art: A balcony with kite string on the railing, a rubber band on the floor, a potted plant, and a bowl of water in the shade.

items.p: Arun, a boy of 5, says, 'The pigeon could break the kite string if she pulled harder.' What would you tell him? Use what you found in the wet loop test.
items.a: Nylon string is a plastic. In the test, the plastic loop only stretched and did not tear, even when wet. So pulling harder would not break it, and it could cut her foot.
items.why: A strong answer uses the plastic loop as evidence, and says that plastic stays strong when wet.

items.p: In the wet loop test, why did we keep one paper loop dry?
opts: To see what the water did to the paper
Because there was not enough water
items.why: The dry loop held and the wet loop tore. The only difference was the water, so the water made the paper weak.

items.p: In the bag-in-the-bucket test, a thin bag drifted in the water. Draw a sea turtle seeing a floating bag and a jellyfish side by side.
items.a: A drawing of a turtle with a puffed-open bag and a jellyfish that look alike.
items.why: A strong drawing shows why the turtle could mix them up: both are thin, pale and drifting.

items.p: Put in order how a wrapper dropped on a road can reach a lake.
items: Rain washes the wrapper into a drain.
Someone drops a wrapper on the road.
The drain water flows into the lake.
A duck finds the wrapper in the lake.
items.why: First the wrapper is dropped, then rain washes it into a drain, the drain flows to the lake, and an animal meets the wrapper there.

items.p: Plastic lasts much longer than paper or banana peels.
items.why: True. Paper and peels rot away in weeks or months. Most plastic lasts many years, breaking only into smaller bits.

items.p: After Sankranti, a family in Ahmedabad talks about kites.

views.says: We should stop flying kites. Birds get hurt every year.
Kite flying is our festival and it makes us happy. We can fly with cotton string and pick up every bit after.
Most birds are hurt by nylon and glass-coated string. Many get hurt in the early morning and evening, when lots of birds are flying.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Why? Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: Any view, with a reason. Hetal is right that birds get hurt. The grandmother is right that the festival matters, and that cotton string and picking up help. The rescuer gives facts that help us choose safer ways.
items.why: A strong answer uses a fact from the unit and is fair to another view.

items.p: Ordinary people are not the government. Say to a grown-up, who writes it down: how can ordinary people still protect animals?
items.a: They can guard nests, look after the trees animals live in, pick up litter, and tell others why the animals matter. Many people working together can protect animals even without special powers.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real thing people can do, and why it helps the animal.

items.p: Label the parts of this lake that are living and the parts that are non-living.
items.a: Living: fish, ducks, frog, lotus. Non-living: water, mud, stones, sunlight.
items.why: A strong answer labels at least three of each.
items.art: A lake with fish, ducks, a frog, lotus plants, water, mud, stones and the Sun above.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Kite string, rubber band, banana peel, mask ear loop.
items.why: The other three are loops or strings that can trap an animal. A banana peel rots away and cannot trap anyone.

items.p: Name one thing your family could do this week to care for the environment. Say why it helps.
items.a: For example: snip every loop before it goes in the bin, so no animal gets trapped. Or carry a cloth bag, so we use fewer plastic bags.
items.why: A strong answer names a real action and says which harm it stops.

opts: Everything around us: air, water, land and all living beings
Only the trees on our street
quiz.why: Our environment is everything around us, living and non-living, including us.

quiz.p: Which of these is a non-living part of the environment?
quiz.why: Water is not alive, but every living being needs it. The sparrow and the tulsi are alive.

quiz.p: What are the two main ways litter harms animals?
opts: They get trapped in it, or they eat it
It makes them too cold, or too hot
It makes them sleep, or sing
quiz.why: Loops and strings trap animals. Bags, caps and wrappers get swallowed.

quiz.p: In a test, a wet paper loop tore at the first pull. What did a wet plastic loop do?
quiz.why: Plastic does not soak up water, so it stays strong when wet. That is why a plastic loop can trap a bird.

quiz.p: Why is plastic litter more dangerous to animals than paper litter?
opts: Plastic stays strong in water and lasts for years
quiz.why: Wet paper goes weak and rots away. Plastic stays strong and lasts, so it can trap or harm animals for a long time.

quiz.p: Why might a sea turtle swallow a floating plastic bag?
opts: The bag drifts like a jellyfish, which turtles eat
quiz.why: A thin bag in water puffs open and drifts like a jellyfish. Many scientists think turtles mix them up.

quiz.p: You find a rubber band in your dry waste. What should you do before it goes in the bin?
quiz.why: A snipped band is a strip, which cannot close round an animal's foot or beak.

quiz.p: Which bag makes the least litter?
opts: A cloth bag used again and again
A new plastic bag each day
A new paper bag each day
quiz.why: A bag used hundreds of times means hundreds fewer bags thrown away.

quiz.p: Village women hear that loggers are coming to cut down their forest. They have no weapons and no power. What could they do that might save the trees?
opts: Hold on to the trees so they cannot be cut down
quiz.why: Standing with the trees means the loggers cannot cut them without hurting people. Many people together, peacefully, are hard to ignore. Women in the Himalayas really did this, and it was called Chipko, 'to hug'.

quiz.p: A rare stork nests in tall trees near villages. People cut the trees and chase the birds away. What would help the storks most?
opts: Village people guarding the nests and the nesting trees
quiz.why: The storks need their nesting trees and peace while they raise their young. People who live nearby can protect both every day.

quiz.p: Nylon kite string is banned in India because it hurts birds and people.
quiz.why: True. In 2017 the National Green Tribunal banned nylon and other plastic kite string across India.

applications: Bird rescue groups in Ahmedabad, Hyderabad, Jaipur and other cities run care camps for birds hurt by kite string at the kite festivals.
Cities like Chennai and Bengaluru ask homes to sort waste into wet and dry, so less waste goes to open dumps where animals feed.
Many Indian states have banned thin plastic carry bags, and India banned many single-use plastic items in 2022.
Volunteers clean beaches and lakes, such as the Versova beach clean-up in Mumbai, which began in 2015.
Village women in Assam protect the nesting trees of the greater adjutant stork.

open_questions.q: How long does a plastic bag really last?
open_questions.why_open: Plastic bags are only about 60 years old, so nobody has watched one for hundreds of years. Scientists make careful guesses, and they do not all agree.

open_questions.q: How often do sea turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists find plastic in many turtles' stomachs, but they cannot easily watch turtles choosing food in the deep sea.

open_questions.q: What do the tiny bits of broken plastic do inside animals, and inside us?
open_questions.why_open: Tiny plastic bits are now found in water, soil, animals and people. Scientists are still finding out how much harm they do.

founder: ideas/by_topic/caring-for-the-environment.md: mostly climate activities for older levels. Its Rachel Carson card is already used in the Level 1 unit, so it is not repeated here.

ideas/by_topic/waste.md: 'Waste is not a waste' week and the reduce-waste-at-home project. Waste sorting, rotting and recycling are taught in the sci.waste units, so this unit keeps to harm to animals and care.

Board chapter: Cambridge Primary Science Stage 2, 1.5 'How can we care for our environment?' (litter harming animals, recycling, protected places, a survey of places near home). The survey is activity a2, and protected places are in the links and the Hargila Army story.

Ladder: sci.environment.caring.L1 (rain carries litter to the drain, ants, caring for a plant) comes before. This unit moves on to what happens when animals meet litter, and why the material matters. It leads to sci.environment.caring.L3 (the living and non-living environment, the closed box) and the pollution and conservation units.
science: Charlton-Howard H. S., Bond A. L., Rivers-Auty J. and Lavers J. L. (2023). 'Plasticosis': characterising macro- and microplastic-associated fibrosis in seabird tissues. Journal of Hazardous Materials. Flesh-footed shearwater chicks on Lord Howe Island; scarring linked to plastic, not to pumice.
National Green Tribunal, order of 11 July 2017, banning nylon and synthetic kite string (manja) across India.

Schuyler Q. and others (2014). Global analysis of anthropogenic debris ingestion by sea turtles. Conservation Biology. Turtles commonly swallow plastic. That they mistake bags for jellyfish is a widely held but still studied explanation.
Chipko: Gaura Devi and the women of Reni village, 1974 (now Uttarakhand).
Purnima Devi Barman and the Hargila Army, Assam: Whitley Award (2017) and UN Champions of the Earth (2022).
Saalumarada Thimmakka planted and cared for banyan trees along about 4 kilometres of road between Hulikal and Kudur, Karnataka.

roots.context: We have tested which wet loops tear and which hold, and learned how litter traps animals. Now we ask what that tells us about the things we throw away and the beings who meet them.

deep_truth.truth: In your bowl, the wet paper loop tore at the first gentle pull. The wet plastic loop only stretched and held. A bird caught in paper can pull free, but not from plastic. So what litter is made of decides how much harm it can do.
deep_truth.habit: We think all litter is the same: just mess that looks untidy. But a wrapper, a peel and a rubber band are not the same to the animal who meets them. The material decides whether it rots away, tears, or traps.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Wet Loop Test, the dry paper held and the wet paper tore, so the water made it weak. The wet cloth and the wet plastic held for all five pulls. In 2023, scientists found that plastic scarred the stomachs of sea bird chicks, while pumice stones did not.

three.who_am_i: You are one of the many animals who share this place. What you drop, another animal meets.
three.what_is_life: A pigeon feels the string tighten and pulls to get free. Plants also sense touch, light and harm, and they respond.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is shared. A lake belongs to the fish, the ducks, the lotus and the people who live by it.

roots.thread: Litter does not stop mattering when it leaves our hand. The litter goes on to meet someone: a cow by the road, a pigeon on a roof, a turtle in the sea. Each of them senses the litter, and decides what to do: eat it, pull against it, or pass it by. What happens next depends on what the litter is made of. So caring for the environment means thinking about the beings who will meet what we leave behind.

teachings.teaching: Look on deer, camels, donkeys, monkeys, mice, snakes, birds and flies as you would look on your own children.
teachings.link: A parent would never leave a trap where their child plays. Snipping a loop is caring for a bird the way we care for our own family.

teachings.source: Karaniya Metta Sutta (Sutta Nipata 1.8), a teaching of the Buddha
teachings.teaching: Whatever living beings there are, weak or strong, big or small, seen or unseen, near or far, may they all be well.
teachings.link: We rarely see the cow at the dump or the turtle in the sea who meets our litter. They are the unseen and far-away beings this teaching asks us to wish well.

science.text: Plastic does not soak up water, so it stays strong when wet. Most plastic lasts many years in water and soil.
How long plastic lasts, and what tiny plastic bits do inside animals, are still being studied.

other_view.view: Some people say that one family snipping loops makes only a small difference. Most plastic litter comes from how things are made, packed and sold, and from places with no proper waste collection. They say laws, companies and good city waste systems matter more than one family's habits. Others reply that families, villages and laws work best together.

practice.title: Feel the Loop
practice.say: Put a rubber band loosely round two of your fingers. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly, three times. Now gently spread your fingers. Feel the band hold them. Think of a bird who feels this round their foot. Now take the band off and snip it open. How does the strip feel now?
practice.kid: Put a rubber band round two fingers. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly three times. Spread your fingers gently. Feel the band hold. Think of a bird's foot. Now snip the band open.

ask: When you throw something away, who do you think meets it next?
Does a cow searching a rubbish heap know which things are safe to eat?
Who does a lake belong to?
roots.art: A girl holding a snipped-open rubber band in her palm, with a pigeon on the railing behind her and a faint lake with a turtle and a cow on the road drawn in the distance.

how_we_found_out.context: How did scientists find out that swallowed plastic hurts sea birds, even when the birds stay alive? This card tells the true story of a team that included a woman scientist from Australia.
how_we_found_out.story: Flesh-footed shearwaters are sea birds who nest on Lord Howe Island, off the coast of Australia. The parents fly over the sea and bring back food for their chicks. But they also pick up floating bits of plastic, and feed those to their chicks too. Scientists found plastic in the stomachs of most of the chicks. For a long time, many people thought that if a chick stayed alive, the plastic did no real harm. Birds swallow small stones too, such as light pumice stones that float on the sea, and the stones seem to do no harm. Jennifer Lavers, an Australian scientist, had studied these birds for years. With Alex Bond, Hayley Charlton-Howard and Jack Rivers-Auty, she looked at the stomachs of chicks under a microscope. In 2023 they reported that plastic left scars inside the stomach. The more plastic, the more scars. Pumice did not leave scars like that. They named the new illness plasticosis. So plastic harms a bird even when the bird does not die.
how_we_found_out.who: Jennifer Lavers, an Australian scientist, with Hayley Charlton-Howard, Alex Bond and Jack Rivers-Auty
how_we_found_out.when: Years of study on Lord Howe Island, and the report in 2023
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people thought that if a sea bird chick swallowed plastic and stayed alive, the plastic did no real harm, like the small stones birds swallow.

playtest: Walked through the unit as a parent and child in a flat. The wet loop test needs only newspaper, an old cloth, a washed milk packet and a bowl of water, and the wet paper tears while the plastic only stretches. The bag-in-the-bucket test now says the bag may not drift every time and what to do then. Fixed the Clean Lake board (the rain track is now 8 written steps), the card deck that ran out before the game could end, and the sorting game that could go on for ever. Added a card telling the Chipko, Hargila Army and Thimmakka stories that the quiz asked about, removed repeated questions and a joke that made no sense, made the maths names clear, and took family members out of the pictures and steps.
